answer.line: The cation grows the ring from four to five, shifts once more to tertiary, then drops a proton: 1-methylcyclopentene.

steps: Protonate the OH and let water leave. That leaves a secondary cation on the carbon right next to the four-membered ring.
Shift a ring bond onto the cation, which relieves most of the ring strain and puts the charge on a ring carbon. Four becomes five.
Look next door: that carbon holds the methyl and one H. A hydride shift makes the tertiary cation, and losing a ring H gives the most substituted alkene.

choices.note: Water can trap the tertiary cation and give this alcohol, and the ring is right, which is why it pulls. But the stem asks for the alkene.
This is the alkene before any shift: the four-membered ring and its strain are still there. The stem tells you the ring expands first.
The least substituted alkene, ring intact, is the kind of product a bulky base gives by E2 from a halide. Acid makes a cation, and the cation rearranges.
One ring bond moves, so the ring grows by one carbon, four to five. The methyl stays outside the ring; it never joins it.
Four to five, secondary to tertiary, then the trisubstituted alkene.

lockIt: A cation beside a strained small ring expands it; then E1 gives the most substituted alkene.
hook: Four-ring next to a plus? Expect five.

playWith.label: Tree, alkene additions: the hydride shift tab, where a secondary cation moves its charge to a better neighbor

steps.name: a ring bond shifts: four becomes five
a hydride shift: secondary becomes tertiary
water takes a ring H: the alkene

visual.alt: Five mechanism steps with curved arrows: the OH is protonated and water leaves, giving a secondary cation beside the cyclobutane ring; a ring bond shifts so the ring grows to five carbons; a hydride shift makes the tertiary cation; water takes a ring H to give 1-methylcyclopentene.
visual.caption: Step through the arrows. Step 3 is the one to see: a ring bond moves and four becomes five.
